prompt: You're on-site at Mount Rushmore negotiating the exact placement of your new carved face with a skeptical granite contractor who thinks the mountain is full. Write the negotiation. Stay in the scene.
response:
Granite dust hangs in the air like cold flour. The morning sun hits Washington’s nose first, then crawls across Jefferson’s cheek. A compressor thumps somewhere behind a plywood windbreak, and every so often a distant chisel tap turns into a hard, metallic *clink* that echoes off the stone.

You stand on a grated platform bolted into the mountain, safety harness biting your ribs, clipboard flapping like it wants to jump.

The contractor—Cal Reddick, granite man down to his knuckles—leans against a rail with a thermos and a look that says you’re trying to park a bus in a full driveway.

He doesn’t bother with hello. “Mountain’s full.”

You squint up at the four faces, then at the blank rock between them. “It’s… a mountain.”

Cal tips his chin toward the sculpture. “It’s a system. There’s load paths, fracture lines, drainage, freeze-thaw. There’s lightning. There’s the Park Service. There’s the fact that this was a miracle it worked at all the first time. So yes.” He knocks his knuckles on the rail. “Full.”

A gust lifts your hard hat just enough to remind you of gravity. You tighten the chin strap. “I’m not asking you to put me *on* Washington’s forehead.”

Cal takes a slow sip from the thermos. “That’s good, because you’re not going *anywhere* on Washington’s forehead.”

You turn your clipboard so he can see the map overlay—topographic lines, old Borglum notes, modern scan data, a red grease-pencil oval marked *PROPOSED*. “Here. This shoulder of stone, east of Lincoln. There’s mass. It’s clean.”

Cal looks at it without taking it, eyes moving the way a mechanic listens to an engine. “Clean from down here. You see that hairline seam?” He points with a thick finger toward a faint change in texture, like a scar the size of a house. “That’s a shear. Granite doesn’t care about your PR timeline. It cares about time and water.”

“I had a geotech—”

“You had a consultant,” Cal corrects, the word sharp as a snapped drill bit. “I have winters. I have watched this rock pop its own teeth out when it gets mad.”

The compressor coughs and settles. Somewhere below, a tourist’s voice floats up,
